what.text: Ketoconazole is an antifungal medicine. It blocks the making of ergosterol, a part of the fungal cell wall.
On the skin and scalp it is used against fungi such as Malassezia, which is linked to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.
Using ketoconazole for hair loss is off-label.

research.text: Evidence for ketoconazole in pattern hair loss is small. A 2020 review found five human studies and said randomized controlled trials are still needed.

research.title: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo versus plain shampoo, with or without minoxidil

facts.v: Controlled comparison of ketoconazole shampoo with an unmedicated shampoo, used with or without minoxidil 2%
Men with pattern hair loss (number not given in the abstract)
Long-term use (length not given in the abstract)
Hair density, hair size, share of growing (anagen) hairs, scalp oil

research.found: Hair density, size and the share of growing hairs improved about the same with the ketoconazole and minoxidil regimens. The authors said a larger controlled study was needed.

research.title: Topical ketoconazole for pattern hair loss

facts.v: 5 human studies (318 people) and 2 animal studies
Hair shaft diameter, hair cycle, photo and self-rated change

research.found: Human studies reported thicker hair shafts and some improvement. The review called for randomized controlled trials.

src.label: Fields et al., Dermatol Ther, 2020 (systematic review)

research.text: The same review reported that two mouse studies found more hair regrowth with ketoconazole than in untreated mice. These results are in animals only.

src.label: Fields et al., Dermatol Ther, 2020 (systematic review)

us.text: FDA has approved ketoconazole products for fungal infections and dandruff, not for hair loss.
Compounded drugs are not FDA approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

src.label: FDA, Compounding and the FDA: Q&A

items.text: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo is approved for tinea versicolor, a fungal skin infection. The brand Nizoral shampoo 2% was approved in 1990 and is now discontinued; generics remain.
Nizoral Anti-Dandruff (ketoconazole 1%) was approved in 1997 and is sold over the counter to control dandruff flaking, scaling and itching.
Ketoconazole 2% cream is approved for ringworm-type infections (tinea), tinea versicolor, skin candidiasis and seborrheic dermatitis.

us.text: Ketoconazole tablets have a boxed warning. They can cause serious liver injury, including deaths and liver transplants, can cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems with some other drugs, and can lower adrenal hormone output. The label says they are not for skin or nail fungal infections and should be used only when other antifungals are not available or tolerated.
FDA records show a priority safety-labeling change to Nizoral tablets approved on July 25, 2013.
No ketoconazole product is FDA approved for hair loss. Compounded hair sprays that contain it are not FDA approved.

world.lead: Topical ketoconazole is an approved antifungal in the US, Canada and the EU. In the EU, oral ketoconazole for fungal infections was suspended in 2013. No regulator we checked has approved it for hair loss.

countries.status: Approved medicine (shampoos and cream for fungal skin conditions and dandruff; 1% shampoo over the counter). Oral tablets restricted under a boxed warning. Not approved for hair loss.
A Nizoral product is marketed as a non-prescription drug. Not approved for hair loss.

after.text: Ketoconazole is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or on the 2027 List, which takes effect January 1, 2027.

side.text: Side effects below come from the US labels for ketoconazole shampoo and cream. No label covers a scalp spray mixed with other drugs.

items.text: In 11 double-blind trials of 2% shampoo (264 people), an increase in normal hair loss and irritation each occurred in under 1%.
Hair discoloration, abnormal hair texture, and oiliness or dryness of hair and scalp have been reported.
Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with the 2% shampoo.
In cream trials, 5% of 905 people reported side effects, mainly severe irritation, itching and stinging. The cream contains a sulfite that can cause allergic-type reactions.

side.text: The serious liver, heart-rhythm and adrenal warnings apply to ketoconazole tablets taken by mouth. EMA says topical forms are absorbed into the body in very low amounts.

unconfirmed: We could not open FDA’s July 2013 Drug Safety Communication on oral ketoconazole (fda.gov returned not found); the page cites the tablet label and FDA’s Drugs@FDA data instead.
The 1998 Piérard-Franchimont study’s number of people and length were not in the abstract, and we could not open the full paper.
We could not confirm ketoconazole’s UK status from an MHRA record; the MHRA products site did not load without scripts.
We could not reach Australia’s TGA (ARTG search failed), so Australia is pending.
The Canadian Nizoral record did not state its dosage form when we checked.
surprises: FDA’s label for ketoconazole 2% shampoo lists an increase in normal hair loss (under 1% of trial users) and abnormal hair texture as side effects, though the shampoo is often promoted for hair loss.
The prescription 2% shampoo label is approved only for tinea versicolor, not dandruff; the dandruff product is the 1% over-the-counter shampoo.
